---
title: "Authentication and Access Control"
subtitle: "Security, Privacy, and Consumer Protection"
author: "Nick Feamster · University of Chicago"
---

## What Access Control Is For {.center}

Four goals that keep showing up — in operating systems, phones, the cloud:

- Protect **users** from each other
- Protect **apps** from each other
- Protect the **system** from the network
- Still **allow sharing** across those boundaries

::: {.notes}
Frame the whole lecture as a tension: isolation versus sharing. Every
mechanism we see — Unix permissions, Android sandboxes, OAuth scopes — is
a different answer to "how do I let things cooperate without letting them
run wild?" The four-goal framing comes from Tanenbaum and Bos, Modern
Operating Systems, chapter 9. Cold-call: where have you personally hit
an access-control wall this week? A "permission denied" from a shared
drive, an app asking for camera access, a 403 from an API. Use two or
three examples to seed the subject/verb/object framing that arrives a
few slides in.
:::

## The Threat Model Has Shifted {.smaller}

Old multi-user OS: machines were **expensive and shared**; apps were **trusted**
because users wrote them.

PC OS: still descends from multi-user OSes — apps run with **the user's full
privileges**.

The smartphone insight: that model would **kill the platform**. Phones were redesigned
from the ground up to run **untrusted apps** from anyone.

::: {.vignette}
"What's old is new again." The web browser is now an OS: a single user running dozens
of **untrusted apps** (web pages, extensions). The cloud — Google Docs, SaaS tenants —
is the new multi-user mainframe. The same access-control problems came back, just with
new names.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the spine of the lecture. Techniques invented for 1970s
timesharing got repurposed for multi-app worlds. Ask: who do you trust on
your phone? Almost no app. Who did a 1975 mainframe user trust? Everyone
with an account, because everyone with an account had submitted their
code through a systems programmer. The browser-as-OS observation is
concrete: Chrome's sandbox design docs describe a per-tab process with
almost no ambient authority, exactly the mainframe user-isolation model
recast for untrusted JavaScript. SaaS multi-tenancy (Google Workspace,
Salesforce) is the new shared mainframe — and the 2025-2026 breach
vignette at the end of the deck is what happens when that isolation
leaks. Fresh browser-as-OS example (Socket, Sept 23, 2026): a Firefox
add-on posing as a "PDF Identity Verifier" shipped clean code, fetched
its payload after store review, used FedCM to find the Google account
already signed in, and drove accounts.google.com to steal the session
cookie — no password ever phished. Brief in speaker-notes, slide 3.
:::

## Who Are You Defending Against?

- **Casual prying** — curiosity, browsing what you shouldn't
- **Insider attacks** — snooping by people who already have access
- **Financial motive** — making money (fraud, ransomware, resale)
- **Espionage** — commercial or state-sponsored data theft
<!-- TODO: consider appending "(2026: China-aligned TA419 impersonated real AI-policy figures to AitM-phish US think tanks — Proofpoint, Oct 1)" to the Espionage bullet; left in notes for now -->

Note the split between **passive** (read-only snooping) and **active** (modifying)
intruders — and between **security** (keep people out) and **privacy** (limit what
even authorized parties learn).

::: {.notes}
Taxonomy from Tanenbaum and Bos chapter 9.1; the passive/active and
security/privacy splits are Saltzer and Schroeder 1975 vocabulary. The
point of naming intruders is that your design changes with the adversary.
Defending against a curious roommate is not the same as defending against
UNC6395 — the threat actor behind the August 2025 Salesloft-Drift OAuth
token theft, whom we'll meet in the closing vignette. For the espionage
row, the Oct 1, 2026 Proofpoint report on TA419 is the live example:
a China-aligned actor impersonating a former White House OSTP deputy
director (and, in Feb 2026, a senior Anthropic employee) to lure US
AI-policy experts onto a Frameless-BitB adversary-in-the-middle page that
relays the real Microsoft login and keeps the session cookie — password
and MFA both succeed. Full brief in speaker-notes, slide 4. Cold-call: pick two
adversary categories and name one control that differs between them
(rate-limiting stops the curious, doesn't stop the espionage-motivated).
:::

## Identification, Authentication, Authorization {.smaller}

Three words students conflate — keep them straight (this is a likely **exam**
distinction):

- **Identification** — *who do you claim to be?* (a username)
- **Authentication** — *prove it.* (a password, key, or biometric)
- **Authorization** — *what are you allowed to do?* (the access-control decision)

The full sequence: **identify & authenticate → authorize → access control →
logging & auditing → accountability.** The first three are *preventive*; the last
two are *reactive* (forensics after the fact).

::: {.notes}
This is a very likely exam distinction — students conflate all three
words. Physical analogy: your ID card identifies you, the guard checking
your face against it authenticates, the list of doors your badge opens is
authorization, the badge-reader log is accountability. The canonical
technical treatment is NIST SP 800-63-4 (finalized July 31, 2025),
especially SP 800-63B, which walks the identify/authenticate/authorize/log
sequence. Access control is often breached, so logging is defense-in-depth,
not an afterthought — the whole point of the Salesloft-Drift breach is
that the audit logs are what told anyone the tokens had been abused.
Two Sept 2026 pieces make "logging is defense-in-depth" concrete: a
Clear Path Security guide (via Security Boulevard, Sept 14) on which
Microsoft 365 audit events expose OAuth consent phishing — consent
grants, new service principals, broad scopes like mail/files/offline_access
— and Microsoft's Sept 9 passkey-lure report, which says to hunt the
*sequence* (new auth method added → Graph recon → bulk SharePoint reads)
rather than any one indicator. Links in speaker-notes, slide 5.
:::

## The Three Modes of Authentication {.smaller}

How do you prove who you are? Exactly three categories (and **MFA** combines them):

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Something you know**

- Passwords, PINs
- Security questions
- *Weakness:* guessed, phished, reused, leaked
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Something you have**

- Phone, hardware key (YubiKey)
- 2FA token, smart card
- *Weakness:* lost, stolen, cloned
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Something you are**

- Fingerprint, face, iris
- *Weakness:* can't be revoked; spoofable; consent & privacy concerns
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Flagged as midterm material in the agenda. Drill the categories with quick
examples: a fingerprint reader on a door is "something you are"; a
concert ticket is "something you have"; a Kerberos password is "something
you know." NIST SP 800-63B section 5 is the canonical reference for
authenticator requirements. Biometrics' fatal property: you can't reset
your fingerprint after a breach — the 2010 National Academies report
"Biometric Recognition: Challenges and Opportunities" laid this out
formally. Legal wrinkle worth flagging: US case law splits on whether
police can compel a biometric unlock (Fifth Amendment questions), whereas
compelled password disclosure has stronger protection.
2026 update for the "something you have" column: SMS codes are being
retired at both ends. Microsoft Entra ID made passkeys the default on
Sept 1, 2026 and retires Microsoft-provided SMS/voice MFA for ordinary
users on Feb 1, 2027 (no opt-out from enforcement); Android 17 (June 2026)
withholds OTP texts from non-default apps for three hours. Say it as:
an SMS code is still "something you have," but no longer counts as
phishing-resistant something-you-have. Brief in speaker-notes, slide 6.
:::
<!-- TODO: consider adding "- *2026:* SMS codes being retired (Entra: Feb 2027)" under "Something you have" — three-column layout is tight, so left to notes -->


## Passwords Are Losing; Passkeys Are Winning {.smaller}

**Why passwords fail.** A password is a **shared secret**: you know it, the server stores it, and anything that sees it once (a phishing page, a keylogger, a breach dump) can use it anywhere you reused it.

**What a passkey is.** Not a secret you know. A **cryptographic key pair** your device makes, **one per site**. The site stores the public half. The private half stays inside your phone, laptop, or security key, unlocked by your face, fingerprint, or PIN.

**How signing in works, in one sentence.** The site sends a random challenge; your device **signs the challenge plus the site's name** with the private key; the site checks the signature with the public key it stored. Nothing typed, nothing reusable sent. (Step by step: next slide.)

**Why that beats a password**

- **Nothing to phish:** no secret leaves the device, and the credential only works for the domain it was made for, so a lookalike site gets nothing useful
- **Nothing to steal from the server:** it holds public keys only
- **Nothing to reuse:** a different key for every site
- **MFA in one gesture:** the key is *something you have*; the unlock is *something you are* or *know*

**Where it stands:** ~5 billion passkeys in use (FIDO Alliance, May 2026); Microsoft Entra made them the default sign-in on Sept 1, 2026 and retires SMS codes Feb 2027; NIST SP 800-63-4 requires a phishing-resistant option at AAL2 and mandates device-bound keys at AAL3.

::: {.notes}
Lead with the contrast: a password is a secret that has to travel; a
passkey is a key that never does. Tie back to the three modes: the
private key is "something you have," unlocked by "something you are or
know," MFA folded into one tap. The mechanics are on the next slide; do
not pre-empt them here beyond the one-sentence version.

Current events for this slide (details and links in speaker-notes.md):
Microsoft Entra passkeys-by-default from Sept 1, 2026, SMS/voice MFA
retiring Feb 1, 2027 (Microsoft Security Blog, Jul 13, 2026);
"Pass-the-Passkey" at Black Hat Aug 2026: malware already on the
endpoint could replay logged WebAuthn assertions or recover Google-synced
private keys; the crypto held, the surrounding infrastructure did not
(The Hacker News, Aug 10, 2026); and Microsoft's Sept 9, 2026 report on
"update your passkey" help-desk lures. Cold-call: what category of attack
does a passkey not stop? Seed: post-auth token abuse, malware on the
endpoint, account-recovery social engineering. NIST SP 800-63-4
(finalized July 31, 2025) is the regulatory anchor.
:::

## How a Passkey Actually Works {.smaller}

A passkey is a **per-site public-key pair** (FIDO2 / WebAuthn). The site keeps the public key; the private key never leaves your authenticator (phone, laptop, security key, or password manager).

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Registration (once per site)**

1. Site sends a random **challenge** + its identity (**relying-party ID** = its domain)
2. Browser asks your authenticator; you unlock it (Face ID, fingerprint, PIN)
3. Authenticator mints a **fresh key pair for this site only**
4. Public key + credential ID go to the site; private key stays put
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Sign-in (every time)**

1. Site sends a new random **challenge**
2. Browser hands challenge + **origin** to the authenticator; you unlock it
3. Authenticator **signs** (challenge, origin, counter) with the private key
4. Site verifies the signature with the stored public key, checks the challenge is the one it sent and the origin is itself
:::
:::

**Why phishing fails:** the browser only offers a credential to the domain it was registered for, and the signature names the origin, so a lookalike site gets nothing it can replay. **Why breaches fail:** the server holds only public keys. **Why replay fails:** every challenge is single-use.

**Synced vs. device-bound:** synced passkeys are copied between your devices by a passkey provider (end-to-end encrypted; recoverable if you lose a phone). Device-bound ones never leave the hardware (NIST AAL3). Cross-device sign-in: scan a QR code, Bluetooth proves the phone is nearby.

::: {.notes}
Draw the two flows on the board as two round trips. The thing students
miss: the private key signs the *origin*, not just the challenge, so the
protection does not depend on the user noticing a lookalike URL. Tie to
the three modes: the key is something you have; the unlock is something
you are or know; one tap does both. Then the Pass-the-Passkey research on
the previous slide reads correctly: malware on the endpoint sits *inside*
the box that holds the private key, so none of the three "why X fails"
lines applies to it.
:::

## A Common Framework: Subject, Verb, Object

Every access-control question reduces to one triple:

> Can **subject** *(a (user, program) pair)* perform **verb** *(an action)*
> on **object** *(a resource)*?

**Exercise:** Consider Facebook. Identify as many **subjects**, **verbs**, and
**objects** as you can.

::: {.notes}
Run this as a 60-second breakout. The (subject, verb, object) triple is
Butler Lampson's 1971 access matrix — the ancestor of every access-control
model in this deck. Seed for Facebook: subjects (you, a friend, the
News Feed ranker, an ad partner, the moderation team); verbs (read, post,
tag, delete, share, download); objects (a photo, a wall, a friend list, a
DM, a group). Note that the same person is different subjects depending on
context (you-the-user vs. you-the-advertiser vs. you-the-page-admin). The
triple is the through-line for the rest of the lecture — Unix, Android,
OAuth all instantiate it.
:::

## ACLs vs. Capabilities {.smaller}

Two fundamentally different ways to store "who can do what":

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Access Control Lists**

*The object knows who may use it.*

- Examples: door fingerprint reader, passport control
- Needs **identity / authentication**
- Easy to **revoke** and change rights
- Delegation is hard
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Capabilities (tokens)**

*Holding the token = having the right.*

- Examples: a house key, a concert ticket
- **No identity needed** → more private
- Just **copy the token** to delegate
- Tokens "**get away from you**" — hard to revoke
:::
:::

Remember this trade-off — **OAuth access tokens are capabilities**, and their
revocation problem will bite us shortly.

::: {.notes}
Foundational reading: Dennis and Van Horn's 1966 paper on programming
semantics for multiprogrammed computations invented capabilities; Miller,
Yee, and Shapiro's 2003 "Capability Myths Demolished" is the modern
defense. The whole second half of the lecture — OAuth, JWTs — is
capabilities on the web. Plant the seed now: capabilities are great for
delegation and privacy (no identity needed to use them, easy to copy),
terrible for revocation (holder can pass them on, no central "who has
this?" registry). That tension is exactly what the 2025 Salesloft-Drift
and 2026 Vercel OAuth breaches exploit — stolen tokens work just as well
as authorized ones.
:::

## Unix: A Simplified ACL Model {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Subject** = a user-space process (runs *as* a user)
- **Verb** = read / write / execute
- **Object** = files — and "file" means a *lot*: sockets, devices, OS functions
- **Root / superuser** owns the system; `sudo` = "super-user do"
- Some services run **as their own user** (e.g. `www-data`, `nobody`) so a compromise
  doesn't own the box
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![`ls -l`: owner, group, world × r/w/x](images/slide012_img004.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This matches the live demo in the agenda: run `ls -l`, `whoami`, `groups`,
and `ps` to show processes running as users. Walk the permission bits
left to right: file type, then three rwx triples for owner, group, and
world. Note that PC OSes are still "multi-user" even with one human —
services like `www-data` and `nobody` get their own UIDs so a compromised
web server doesn't own the machine. That's the hack of repurposing a
1970s multi-user feature (Unix on PDP-11) for an untrusted-app world.
Sets up the next slide on least privilege directly.
:::

## The Principle of Least Privilege {.smaller}

> Grant **only the minimum privileges** needed to do the task — and no more.

- Web servers run as **`www-data`/`nobody`**, not root, so a bug doesn't hand over the
  whole machine
- A **privilege-escalation** attack is precisely a flaw that lets a low-privilege
  process gain higher rights
- The same idea reappears as **OAuth scope** — give an app *read playlists*, not
  *full account access*
- **Real case:** an over-permissive GitHub-Actions→AWS deploy role let **UNC6426** go from one
  stolen npm-delivered GitHub token to **AWS `AdministratorAccess` in < 72 hours** — every API
  call authorized ([Google Cloud Threat Horizons H1 2026, p. 24](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/cloud_threat_horizons_report_h12026.pdf))

This single principle ties the OS half and the OAuth half of this lecture together.

::: {.notes}
Least privilege is Saltzer and Schroeder principle #4 from their 1975
paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems" — the most
exam-able design principle in the deck. Historical hook: pre-2000 Apache
often ran as root, so any RCE handed the whole box to the attacker;
dropping to `www-data` after binding port 80 became the standard fix. The
same idea reappears as OAuth scope — read playlists, not manage account.
Cold-call: name a phone app that asks for a permission it doesn't need
for its actual function. The over-permissioned flashlight app is the
canonical answer; contacts-hungry games and cameras-hungry keyboards are
the modern ones. The UNC6426 case (Google Cloud Threat Horizons H1 2026,
Mandiant IR): a QUIETVAULT npm package stole a developer's GitHub PAT; a
CI/CD secrets tool (NORDSTREAM) abused the GitHub-to-AWS OIDC trust to mint
STS credentials for a CloudFormation deploy role; that role had standing
permission to create IAM roles, so one stack later the attacker owned
AdministratorAccess, read S3, terminated prod EC2/RDS, and made every
internal repo public. Google's fix list is Saltzer–Schroeder verbatim:
remove standing iam:CreateRole / iam:AttachRolePolicy, go just-in-time
with a second approval. Full brief in speaker-notes, slide 11.
:::

## Phones: Per-App Sandboxes {.smaller}

Android applies the same triple, but **each app gets its own user ID**:

- **Subjects:** apps (atop a Linux kernel)
- **Objects:** files, other apps, camera, telephony, personal data
- **Verbs:** each resource defines its own (an app declares them in its **manifest**)

Early Android dumped **hundreds of permissions** on users at install time — nobody read
them, *including developers*. The model got coarser (permission *groups*) and then
**just-in-time**.

- **Android 17 (June 2026):** local-network access becomes a **runtime permission**; a system
  **contact picker** replaces blanket `READ_CONTACTS`; OTP texts hidden from non-default apps for
  3 h ([Android Developers Blog, Jun 16, 2026](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/06/Android-17.html))

::: {.notes}
The original Android permission model is the cautionary tale: too many
decisions (principals x actions x objects) overwhelms users. Felt et al.'s
CCS 2011 paper "Android Permissions Demystified" showed that developers
over-requested and users didn't read — the model failed both ends. The
Android Application Sandbox docs describe the per-app UID isolation
underneath. Coarsening into permission groups helped a little; the real
fix was changing when you ask, which is what Android 6.0 (October 2015)
adopted after iOS proved it worked. Segue directly to the iOS prompt on
the next slide.
:::

## Make the Action the Permission {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
The iOS move: don't front-load a wall of permissions. Ask **at the moment of use**, in
**context**, with a reason the user can infer.

- "Why does Uber want my camera?" → because you tapped *scan my credit card*
- Grant **only when needed**, not forever
- Combine the user's *action* with the *permission grant* in one tap
- **Android 17 (2026)** ships this as a system-drawn **location button**: one tap = precise
  location *for this session only* ([Google Security Blog, May 12, 2026](https://blog.google/security/whats-new-in-android-security-privacy-2026/))

This **emphasizes action over configuration** — and leans on sensible **defaults**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Just-in-time permission prompt](images/slide054_img018.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the usability payoff of the lecture: access control fails when it
demands too many up-front decisions. Apple's developer docs on requesting
access to protected resources codify the pattern — ask only at the moment
of use, with a purpose string the user can evaluate. The Uber
"scan my credit card" story is the classic teaching example: combining
the user's action with the permission grant in one tap makes least
privilege the default. Same lesson the web learned with OAuth consent
screens — which is exactly where the second half of the lecture goes.
Android 6.0 (October 2015) adopted the same runtime-permission model.
Counter-example worth 30 seconds: iOS 27 (Sept 2026) shipped a Siri that
reads app content, and EFF's Sept 18 guide maps where the toggles stop —
per-app "Show Content in Search" can be turned off, but EFF reports no
switch exists for on-screen awareness. Ask: when the subject is the OS's
own assistant, who is the prompt protecting you from? Speaker-notes,
slide 13.
:::

# Delegated Access on the Web: OAuth 2.0 {.center}

How do I let an app act *for* me — without handing it my password?

## Life Before OAuth: Just Share the Password {.smaller}

The bad old pattern: a third-party app asks for your **actual username and password**.

- It gets **full control**, not limited access
- No way to **scope** what it can touch
- No clean way to **revoke** it (you'd have to change your password)
- Terrible **auditability** — every action looks like *you*

This is the **capability problem** at internet scale: sharing a credential is sharing
*everything*, forever.

::: {.notes}
Agenda example: banking aggregators like early Mint and pre-open-banking
Plaid used to ask for your actual bank username and password, then screen-
scrape your account. The CFPB's Personal Financial Data Rights rule
(Rule 1033, October 2024) formalized OAuth-style token access for US
financial data — though the 2025 rule status has been contested, so verify
before lecturing. Cold-call: have you ever pasted one service's password
into another app? What could that app then do? The answers — transfer
money, change your recovery email, delete everything — motivate the
delegation problem that OAuth exists to solve.
:::

## What OAuth 2.0 Actually Is {.smaller}

- A **delegation protocol over HTTP** for *limited* access to resources
- Lets an app act on your behalf **without seeing your credentials**
- A **framework, not a full protocol** — it does **not** mandate token format or
  crypto (implementations choose)
- Separates **authentication** ("prove who you are" — to the auth server) from
  **authorization** ("this app may do these things")

The app only ever holds a **token** — a capability that can be **scoped, expired, and
revoked**.

::: {.notes}
Canonical spec is RFC 6749 (October 2012); OAuth 2.1 is in draft and
consolidates the security best-current-practice (mandatory PKCE, no
implicit flow). Emphasize "framework not protocol" — it's why deployments
differ, why so many go wrong, and why every OAuth breach starts with a
sentence like "the vendor implemented step 3 incorrectly." OAuth is
authorization; "log in with Google" is OpenID Connect, layered on top.
The one sentence to leave with students: the token, not your password, is
what crosses the wire to the app — and that token can be scoped, expired,
and (in principle) revoked.
:::

## The Four Roles {.smaller}

| Role | Who it is | Slack + GitHub example |
|---|---|---|
| **Resource owner** | the user who owns the data | you |
| **Client** | the third-party app | Slack |
| **Authorization server** | issues tokens after consent | GitHub's OAuth server |
| **Resource server** | holds data, validates tokens | GitHub's API |

::: {.notes}
The agenda flags this as a midterm question: given a scenario like
Slack plus GitHub, identify the four OAuth roles. RFC 6749 section 1.1
is the canonical definition. Drill it both directions — give a role,
have the class name it; name a party, have them identify the role. The
live demo per the agenda is wiring up the Slack GitHub integration in
class. Common student mistake: conflating "authorization server" and
"resource server" when the same vendor runs both (Google, GitHub) — they
are logically distinct even when co-located.
:::

## The Flow, Six Steps {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
1. Client asks the resource owner for access
2. User logs in & **approves** → gets an **authorization grant** (short code)
3. Client sends the grant + its **client credentials** to the auth server
   (server-to-server, not via the user)
4. Auth server validates → issues an **access token**
5. Client presents the token to the **resource server**
6. Resource server validates → returns the **protected resource**

When the short-lived token expires, a **refresh token** renews it without re-prompting.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![OAuth 2.0 abstract flow](images/slide032_img011.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the diagram with the printing-service-to-Google-Drive story: you
click "let PrintCo print my docs," you land on Google, you consent, Google
sends a short code back to PrintCo, PrintCo trades it (with its own
secret) for an access token, and only then does PrintCo touch your files.
This is the Authorization Code Grant flow, RFC 6749 section 4.1; refresh
tokens are section 6; PKCE for public clients is RFC 7636. Key teaching
point: the client never sees your password, and the grant-for-token
exchange happens server-to-server with client credentials, so a leaked
redirect URL alone shouldn't yield a working token.
:::

## A Real OAuth Flow: Strava API {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Strava OAuth authorization flow](images/slide035_img012.png)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
The same six steps, concrete:

- Athlete clicks **log in**, lands on Strava's consent page
- If they **authorize**, the developer gets an **authorization code + scope**
- Developer exchanges the code for a **short-lived access token + refresh token**
- Now the app can call the API for that athlete's data

**Assignment 2** is exactly this: build a third-party app against any OAuth API
(GitHub, Google Calendar, Nest, Strava…).
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Point at the two consent-screen branches: authorize vs. don't authorize.
The scope shown on that screen is least privilege in action — and it's
what the user is actually consenting to, in plain language. Tie to the
GitHub personal-access-token demo where you pick read-only vs. full repo
scopes, or to GitHub's fine-grained tokens (generally available since
March 2025). Strava's OAuth documentation is the model for the OAuth
activity handout. Assignment 2 is exactly this pattern — students build a
third-party app against any OAuth API (GitHub, Google Calendar, Nest,
Strava) and turn in the scope selection with a justification.
:::

## Tokens: Scope Is Least Privilege {.smaller}

- An **access token = delegated rights**, bounded by **scope** and **duration**
- It's a **capability**: opaque to the client, "bearer" — *whoever holds it, wins*
- Pick the **narrowest scope** that works: *read playlists*, not *manage account*;
  a GitHub PAT with *read-only*, not *repo + admin*
- **Short expiry + refresh tokens** limit the blast radius of a leak

**JSON Web Tokens (JWT)** are the common format: `header.payload.signature` —
self-contained **claims** (issuer, audience, expiry), **signed** so the resource server
can validate **statelessly** (HS256 shared secret, or RS256 public key).

::: {.notes}
Connect back to the ACL-vs-capability slide: tokens are capabilities, so
revocation is the hard part — hence short lifetimes and refresh tokens.
JWT (RFC 7519) is the common format: `header.payload.signature`. HS256
uses a shared secret; RS256 uses a public/private keypair so the resource
server can validate without holding the signing key. The Auth0 explainer
on signing algorithms is a useful student reference. Flip side: JWT lets
you validate statelessly, but you can't easily un-issue one before it
expires — which is why token lifetimes for anything sensitive should be
measured in minutes, not weeks.
:::

## When OAuth Goes Wrong {.smaller}

The protocol is sound; **implementations** leak:

- **Token theft / leakage** — tokens in logs, URLs, browser history; bearer tokens
  need no password to replay
- **CSRF on the redirect** — mitigate with the **`state`** parameter
- **Redirect-URI manipulation** — require **exact match**, never prefix matching
- **Over-broad scope** — violates least privilege; minimize what you request
- **Trusting the other side (AI agents, Sept 2026)** — the official **MCP Python SDK** let a
  malicious MCP server choose the *authorization server*, so the client shipped its **client
  secret + auth code + PKCE verifier** to the attacker; two sibling MCP auth bugs in the same
  month ([GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99, Sept 28, 2026](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99))
- **Defenses:** TLS everywhere, exact redirect matching, `state`, short scopes, never
  log tokens

::: {.notes}
The auth server is a single point of failure — compromise it and
everything downstream falls. Reference the OAuth 2.0 Threat Model
(RFC 6819) and the updated Security Best Current Practice (BCP 240 draft).
The `state` parameter defense is called out explicitly in RFC 6749
section 10.12; redirect-URI exact match is section 4.1 of BCP 240. This
slide sets up the closing vignette: the 2025-2026 breaches weren't OAuth
being "broken." They were stolen bearer tokens being replayed — exactly
the revocation and least-privilege weaknesses we've been flagging all
lecture. The MCP bullet is the agent-permissions thread from last week
with a CVE attached: Cycode found that if the MCP server answers the
modern discovery request with a 404, the SDK falls back to accepting the
server's own login configuration unverified, with the issuer spoofed to
the victim's real provider; the user sees the genuine login page, approves,
and the SDK posts code + client secret + PKCE verifier to the attacker's
token endpoint — PKCE can't help when the verifier is stolen too. Fixed
in 1.30.0 / 2.2.0 (machine-to-machine providers must also pass issuer=).
WorkOS (Oct 2) counts three MCP auth bugs in 30 days with one root cause
— trusting metadata the other party supplied: rmcp CVE-2026-63127 (resource
field unchecked, CVSS 8.2) and LiteLLM CVE-2026-59822 (fabricated
Authorization header → empty auth object, CISA KEV Sept 2). Point back to
step 3 of the flow: right protocol, attacker-supplied address. Full brief
in speaker-notes, slide 21.
:::

## 2025–26: Attackers Stopped Stealing Passwords {.smaller}

::: {.vignette}
**August 2025 — the Salesloft–Drift breach.** Threat actor **UNC6395** stole **OAuth
access + refresh tokens** from the Salesloft Drift chatbot integration and *replayed*
them via the Salesforce API to exfiltrate data from **700+ organizations** (Cloudflare,
Google, Palo Alto Networks, Zscaler, PagerDuty, Proofpoint, Tanium, and more) between
Aug 9–17 — **without ever tripping MFA**, because a valid bearer token needs no second
factor. **April 2026:** the same playbook hit **Vercel** via a compromised **Context.ai
OAuth grant** into a Vercel engineer's Google Workspace, leading to stolen NPM/GitHub
tokens and a **$2M ransom demand**. Meanwhile, AiTM phishing kits (**Tycoon 2FA**,
**EvilProxy**, **EvilTokens**) sent **20M+ Microsoft-365-targeted messages per month**
in 2026.
:::

The lesson of the whole lecture in one breach: **tokens are capabilities** — silent,
bearer, hard to revoke. Defenses that worked on passwords (MFA, login monitoring) don't
see a replayed token. **Scope tightly, expire fast, monitor token use.**

**Fall 2026 update — the playbook is now a product.** **NovaCookies** sells Microsoft 365
session-cookie capture as a **$320/month** service (755 domains; [Island, Aug 26, 2026](https://www.island.io/blog/novacookies-at-scale-inside-the-320-phishing-service-targeting-hundreds-of-organizations));
help-desk callers use *"update your passkey"* as the pretext for AiTM / device-code session theft
([Microsoft, Sept 9, 2026](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/09/09/passkey-themed-social-engineering-leads-identity-cloud-compromise/));
and **Klue** (June 2026) replayed the Salesloft pattern through an abandoned-but-still-valid
credential ([CSO Online](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4187907/klue-breach-exposed-salesforce-crm-data-through-stolen-oauth-tokens.html)).

::: {.notes}
Freshest, most load-bearing example in the deck — figures verified this
session. Salesloft-Drift primary sources: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence
report on UNC6395, and Mitiga's ShinyHunters recap. Cloudflare disclosed
104 stolen Salesforce Case API tokens. Vercel/Context.ai primary: Vercel's
own April 2026 security incident knowledge-base article; CEO Guillermo
Rauch confirmed the $2M BreachForums ransom on X. Tycoon 2FA: Microsoft
Security Blog "Inside Tycoon2FA" (March 4, 2026) — Microsoft blocked over
13 million Tycoon 2FA messages in October 2025 alone. Drive home why it
matters here: every earlier idea converges — capability tokens, least
privilege, revocation, auth server as single point of failure. Cold-call:
would a passkey have stopped Salesloft-Drift? No — the token was already
issued, this is post-auth abuse. Would it have stopped Vercel? Also no —
the OAuth grant was legitimate; the user was compromised via infostealer.
Fall 2026 additions (briefs in speaker-notes, slide 22): NovaCookies is
a subscription AiTM service — relays the real M365 login, passes MFA
through, keeps the session cookie; Island tied it to hundreds of targeted
orgs, ~half US, 90% on .vu domains, infrastructure surging from mid-May
2026. Microsoft's Sept 9 report (Storm-3121 / Storm-3032, since May 2026):
IT-help-desk calls about a passkey/MFA/SSO "update," then AiTM or
device-code token issuance, attacker-added auth methods, Graph recon, and
slow exfil under 1,000 files/hour. Klue (June 2026): a prototype
credential never deactivated → code injected into the Salesforce
integration → customers' OAuth access + refresh tokens harvested (Huntress,
Recorded Future confirmed); Salesforce disabled the integration. Salesloft
status: Salesforce's May 4, 2026 page still says Drift "will remain
disabled until further notice"; class actions pending, no settlement found.
Add to the cold-call: would a passkey stop NovaCookies? Yes — that is the
one case tonight where it would. Would it stop the passkey-lure? No — the
lure never enrolls a passkey.
:::

## Stepping Back: Timeless Design Principles {.smaller}

The 1975 Saltzer–Schroeder principles still hold:

- **Public design** — no security through obscurity
- **Default is "no access"** — fail closed
- **Check current authority** — at *time of use*, not just time of check
- **Least privilege** — the recurring theme
- Build security into the **lowest layers** possible

Classic exploits violated these: **TOCTTOU** races (check vs. use gap), **core-dump
overwrites** of `/etc/passwd`, and **timing attacks** (TENEX: align a password guess
across a page boundary, time the abort).

::: {.notes}
Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) is required reading — the 50-year-old
principles list still holds. TOCTTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) is
formalized in Bishop and Dilger 1996; the TENEX timing attack is written
up in Ross Anderson's Security Engineering, chapter 6. The TENEX story is
a lovely one: the OS aborted password comparison on the first wrong
character, so an attacker who aligned the password guess across a virtual-
memory page boundary could time the abort — page fault or not — and leak
the password one character at a time. Same root cause as modern side
channels like Spectre and Meltdown. TOCTTOU connects directly to "check
current authority" — the gap between check and use is where the exploit
lives. 2026 instance of each principle, all from earlier slides: "check
current authority" — Entra accepting a replayed WebAuthn assertion with no
challenge freshness or session binding (Pass-the-Passkey, slide 7);
"default no access" — the standing iam:CreateRole permission on a CI/CD
role (UNC6426, slide 11); "least privilege" — Klue's prototype credential
that outlived its purpose (slide 22). Speaker-notes, slide 23.
:::

## Scaling Access Control: Abstractions {.smaller}

The matrix of (subject × verb × object) is enormous and mostly empty — so we abstract:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Sparse storage** — default deny; store only the allowed triples as a list
  (Google Docs: millions of users × docs, but each user touches only a few)
- **Roles & groups** — assign rights to a *role*, not each person (corporate projects,
  collaborations)
- **Classification levels** — Bell–LaPadula: *no read up, no write down*
- **Lattices** — when clearances don't form a strict order (Secret-nuclear vs.
  Secret-bio are incomparable)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Protection domains: (object, rights) pairs](images/slide051_img017.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Usability is the real constraint: too many decisions and users click
through everything. Roles, defaults, and just-in-time prompts all exist
to shrink the decision load. Bell-LaPadula (1973 report) is the classic
"no read up, no write down" model; Denning's 1976 paper generalized it to
lattices for cases where clearances don't form a strict order — being
cleared for Secret-nuclear gives you no biological clearance, hence a
partial order, not a line. Modern practice worth naming: Google's Zanzibar
(2019) drives access-control decisions for G Suite sharing at planet
scale — an existence proof that the matrix problem is solvable when you
push it hard enough.
:::

# Wrapping Up {.center}

- One framework — **subject, verb, object** — from Unix to Android to OAuth
- **Least privilege** is the throughline; **revocation** is the hard part
- **OAuth tokens are capabilities** — and 2025–26 proved attackers know it

::: {.notes}
Land the plane: the exam-able core is the three authentication modes,
Unix permissions, least privilege, the four OAuth roles plus flow, and
scope as the operational form of least privilege. The 2025-2026 breach
vignette is the "why it matters today" — every mechanism in the deck
converges on that story. Preview Assignment 2: build a third-party OAuth
app against any provider, submit with scope justification. Next theme is
DoS and botnets — the point where availability becomes the security
property under attack. Debate paired with this material is Data Breaches;
small-group breakout is "Modern Authentication and Access Control."
:::
